title: Hash-Based Indexing
lead: Follow how a hash index assigns keys to buckets, then see how the buckets and directory change as data is added.
goals: Explain in-memory hashing and collision resolution
Trace searches, insertions, deletions, and overflow in static chained hashing
Recognise skew and identify when rehashing is needed
Simulate global and local depth, bucket splits, and directory changes in extendible hashing

sections.title: Ask the right questions of a hash index
sections.html:
A hash index applies a hash function to assign each key to a bucket, a storage area for entries with the same hash address. Two keys in the same bucket must still be compared directly. This approach suits equality lookups, which search for a key with a particular value. For a range query, keys that are close in value need not be close together after hashing.

Original worked example: divide each ticket code by 4 and use the remainder as its bucket number. In compact notation, h(k)=k mod 4, where k is the ticket code and h(k) is a bucket number from 0 to 3. Codes 6, 10, and 14 all enter bucket 2. Finding code 10 requires checking the entries in that bucket; finding every code from 6 to 14 cannot be done by reading bucket 2 alone. Chaining links entries into a list; open addressing searches for another slot in an in-memory table. In a database, a bucket commonly occupies one or more pages.

A small in-memory open-addressing trace

Use an explicitly chosen linear-probing toy policy: four initially empty slots numbered 0–3, h(k)=k mod 4, and no deletions. If the home slot is occupied, try the next slot, wrapping from 3 to 0.

  1. Insert 6: its home slot is 2, so store 6 there.
  2. Insert 10: slot 2 contains 6, so store 10 in the next slot, 3.
  3. Insert 14: slots 2 and 3 are occupied, so wrap and store 14 in slot 0.

The slots now contain [14, empty, 6, 10]. To find 14, start at its home slot 2, compare with 6, then with 10 in slot 3, then find 14 in slot 0. The lookup follows the same probe rule as insertion. This trace illustrates one collision policy; other open-addressing policies use different probe sequences. Deletion needs its own policy so it does not break a later lookup’s probe chain.

Key takeaway

The same hash does not mean the same key. Hashing narrows down where to look; key comparisons are still needed to confirm a match.

Related source material: PDF pages 2–6. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

sections.title: Static hashing: overflow determines the cost
sections.html:
Keep h(k)=k mod 4 and a fixed set of 4 primary bucket pages, each holding 2 entries. Inserting 6 and 10 fills bucket 2; inserting 14 requires an overflow page linked to it. A search for 14 hashes to bucket 2, checks 6 and 10, then follows the link to find 14. If both pages are uncached, it reads 2 pages even though the hash function runs once. Deleting 14 follows the same search path and removes its entry; insertion and deletion must write any modified pages. The empty overflow page can then be reclaimed under the implementation’s policy. Growth lengthens chains; shrinking can leave buckets empty.

State exactly what a hash lookup costs

In the static index’s bucket-access model, an uncached lookup without overflow reads one primary bucket page. Modifying that page requires a read and a write, totaling two I/Os before other overhead. With one primary page and two overflow pages, a failed search can require all three reads. If entries contain RIDs, retrieving table records costs additional I/O: the one-I/O bucket estimate does not promise a one-I/O SELECT of complete rows. An extendible index may also need directory reads unless its directory is resident in memory.

Rehashing recalculates the location of every entry using a new bucket mapping. Increasing the number of buckets redistributes the data but requires many page reads and writes. A fast hash function is not enough: a skewed key distribution or many duplicate keys can still create hot spots. The modulo function above is an illustration, not the best choice for every dataset.

For nonnegative keys, k mod 16 retains the lowest four bits: 0,16,32,48 all enter bucket zero. Changing the modulus or using a better mixing function can address patterns among distinct keys, but cannot spread repeated copies of one key under ordinary key-based partitioning. A good function balances computation with distribution; a prime modulus does not prove collisions impossible.

Related source material: PDF pages 7–12. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

Original supplementary explanation and practice. Sources: Lecture 10 · physical PDF pp. 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12.

sections.title: Extendible hashing: grow where space is needed
sections.html:
Extendible hashing uses a directory, a table of pointers to buckets. The global depth g is the number of hash bits used to look up a directory entry; the local depth d is the number of bits that identify a particular bucket. The example below uses the trailing bits, or suffix.

Original worked example: g=2 gives 4 directory pointers labelled 00, 01, 10, and 11. Bucket 01 has d=2, capacity 2, and hash values 1 (001) and 5 (101). Inserting 9 (1001) would overflow it. Since d=g, first double the directory to g=3: both 001 and 101 temporarily point to the old bucket, and the other old pointers likewise acquire two directory labels. Split that bucket using the last 3 bits and set both new local depths to d=3. Pointer 001 now leads to [1,9]; pointer 101 leads to [5]. Other buckets are unchanged. The completed directory has 8 pointers, and every bucket has d≤g.

Here U00, U10, and U11 name the unchanged targets of the other old pointers; those targets need not be distinct.

Old pointer (g=2)Old targetNew pointers and targets (g=3)
00U00000→U00; 100→U00
01[1,5], d=2001→[1,9], d=3; 101→[5], d=3
10U10010→U10; 110→U10
11U11011→U11; 111→U11
Key takeaway

Doubling the directory enlarges only the pointer table. This step splits the full bucket; it does not copy every data bucket.

If the bucket has d<g before splitting, the directory already has enough bits to distinguish the two new buckets, so only the relevant pointers change. For example, with g=3 and d=1, the remaining 2 bits have 4 combinations, so 4 pointers refer to that bucket. In general, the number of pointers is 2^(g−d). Deletion may allow buckets to merge and the directory to shrink when the structural conditions permit it.

Keep local and global depths consistent

Splitting increments local depth and redirects pointers. If it would exceed the old global depth, double the directory in the same update; the completed index must have d≤g. Buddy buckets share their trailing d−1 bits, differ in the added distinguishing bit, and have equal local depth. They may merge if their combined entries fit. Shrinking must preserve every required distinction; one deletion or empty slot is insufficient evidence.

Delete 9: can this split be reversed?

Bucket 001 now contains [1] and buddy 101 contains [5]. Both have d=3; their shared two-bit suffix is 01 and their two entries fit one bucket. Merge to [1,5] with d=2 and redirect both pointers. All other buckets stayed at their old depths, at most 2, so the directory can drop the extra bit and return to g=2 with four pointers.

Related source material: PDF pages 13–25. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

Original supplementary explanation and practice. Sources: Lecture 10 · physical PDF pp. 15, 25.

sections.title: Check your understanding with a trace
sections.html:
With global depth g=3 and a bucket whose local depth is d=1, how many pointers refer to that bucket? Does splitting it once require doubling the directory?

Show the solution

There are 2^(3−1)=4 pointers. After the split, each new bucket has d=2 and receives 2 pointers. No doubling is needed because 2≤3. If several keys have exactly the same complete hash value, adding bits cannot separate them; a practical implementation needs a separate way to handle this case.

Related source material: PDF pages 15–25. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

quiz.question: A bucket with local depth 2 and global depth 4 is split into buckets with local depth 3. Which statement is correct?
options: The directory does not need to double
quiz.explanation: The new local depth, 3, still does not exceed the global depth, 4.
